inline.s: [All dharmas as Suchness] All dharmas are neither two nor different.
Suchness,
here means sameness.
Śāriputra, in a past age there was a foolish man who did not recognize monkeys. He entered a great forest and saw a troop of monkeys gathered together in one place

This man had heard of the Trāyastriṃśa heavens, so he took them for the Trāyastriṃśa gods. Forthwith he left the forest and returned to his own village, and among a great throng he spoke thus: Have you ever seen the Trāyastriṃśa gods? The people answered, We have never seen them. At once he said: I have seen them; do you wish to see them? All said they wished to. Then he led the crowd to that forest and pointed at the troop of monkeys: Behold, these are the Trāyastriṃśa gods. But the people all said: These are not the Trāyastriṃśa gods; these are monkeys that delight to dwell in the forest. Because you are foolish and inverted, you do not recognize monkeys, and you do not recognize the Trāyastriṃśa gods either. Śāriputra, this man led the crowd to that forest in vain.

tree-

Have you ever seen the Trāyastriṃśa gods?
The people answered

Then he said:
I have seen them; do you wish to see them?
They all said they wished to. So he led the crowd to this forest and, pointing at the troop of monkeys, said:
Look, these are the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
The people
all said
These are not the Trāyastriṃśa gods; these are monkeys playing in the forest. You are foolish and inverted, and you not only fail to recognize the monkeys
for what they are,
but
you also
do not recognize the Trāyastriṃśa gods
for what they are (this is a simile for those who do not recognize the Three Jewels)
Śāriputra, this man led the crowd to that forest in vain.
[Celestial beings (tiānzǐ)] The divine beings of the heavens.

Thus, Śāriputra, in a future age there will be a bhikṣu who goes to the house of a layman and says: Do you wish to see the Buddha and the holy assembly and hear the Dharma? Among them, the laymen who have faith in the Dharma all say they wish to see and hear the Dharma.

Just like the foolish man who did not recognize the Trāyastriṃśa gods, Śāriputra, in a future age there will be a bhikṣu who does not recognize the Dharma and goes among the lay people (white-robed) and says:
Do you wish to see the Buddha and the holy assembly, and hear the Dharma?
Among them, the
lay people who
believe in the Dharma
will all say
“We wish to see the Buddha and the holy assembly and hear the Dharma.

Śāriputra, among them there are laymen who delight in speech and enter the temples. There are bhikṣus fond of talk who are versed in the scriptures, relying on speech and delighting in ornamentation. Those śramaṇas comply and preach to them, calling it the true path. They only fill out the number like cowherds; they only delight in reciting the scriptures without entering the real truth, only pleasing others, valuing fame and profit, skilled in worldly affairs, preaching impurely, capable only of clever words, practicing the worldly path, without any majesty, destroying the cause of nirvāṇa, forsaking the noble silence, not delighting in meditation, day and night always fond of discussion and disputation, sleeping on thick cushions, without even a single thought that accords with meditation, much less attaining the fruit of a śramaṇa. Such a person sleeps always in accord with the worldly mind, and does not cultivate acquiescent patience in the first and last watches of the night, delighting in inferior dharmas.
Śāriputra, among them there are laymen who delight in speech and
enter the temples, where there are many bhikṣus fond of talk who are versed in the scriptures, relying
on
speech and delighting
in the ornamentation of words. Thereupon
these śramaṇas
comply
with those who delight in speech and preach to them, saying this is the true path.
In fact

these śramaṇas merely fill out the number, like cowherds (as a cowherd who has no cows of his own, a simile for those who preach the path without knowing it or practicing it). They only delight in reciting the scriptures and do not
actually practice,

only pleasing others, greedy for fame and profit, skilled at managing worldly human relations, preaching impurely, relying only on eloquent words, practicing the worldly path (secularizing and vulgarizing the Dharma), without any majesty,
destroying the cause of nirvāṇa, for-
-saking
the noble
Dharma and stillness

, not delighting in meditation, day and night always fond of discussion and disputation, greedy for comfort and ease. They do not have even a single thought that accords with meditation, much less attain the fruit of a śramaṇa! Such a person is greedy for sleep, always in accord with the worldly mind, and does not cultivate acquiescent patience in the first and last watches of the night, delighting in inferior dharmas

[First watch and last watch] In ancient Indian reckoning of time, a day and night was divided into six periods: three by day and three by night. The three day periods are dawn, noon, and sunset; the three night periods are the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch. Thus one period equals roughly four modern hours, and six periods equal the modern twenty-four hours. The middle watch corresponds roughly to ten in the evening to two in the morning. The first watch corresponds roughly to six in the evening to ten at night, and the last watch roughly to two in the morning to six.

Such a person also receives much in the way of offerings of clothing and food. Why is that? Because such a person is constantly held by the evil māras, delights in shallow and near words, cannot diligently study the ultimate meaning, cannot recite and uphold the profound scriptures of ultimate meaning, is frightened and terrified upon hearing them, and forsakes the rich essence to take the dregs. There are many ordinary people who, upon seeing their profit and support, give rise to a mind of craving and think: We too should study these discourses.
Such a person also receives much in the way of offerings of clothing and food. Why is that? Such a person is constantly held by the evil māras, delights
in
shallow
and near
words; he cannot diligently study the ultimate meaning, cannot recite and uphold the profound scriptures of the
ultimate
meaning, and upon hearing them is frightened and terrified, for-
-saking the essence
to take the dregs. There are many ordinary people who, upon seeing that they gain much
fame and
profit, give rise to a mind of craving and think: We too should study these discourses and thereby gain both fame and profit.

Śāriputra, such a person forsakes the unsurpassed Dharma treasure and falls into wrong views. He is a caṇḍāla among śramaṇas. There are many laymen who come to him, and such an evil person preaches the Dharma to them. For the sake of profit he praises the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, only seeking a living as a slave of wealth, greedy for clothing and food, praising what he himself delights in:
If one practices giving, one is reborn in heaven.

In the Dharma of the Buddha, giving is an inferior dharma, yet he praises it as supreme and says: The conditions of great giving lead to rebirth in heaven. He does not understand the words and does not comprehend the meaning, knowing only the shallow and near inferior dharma of the first stage, clinging to self and person, and forsaking the ultimate meaning.
Śāriputra, these people who do not recognize the Dharma for-
-sake
the unsurpassed Dharma treasure and fall
into
wrong views. They are evil men among the śramaṇas (caṇḍālas). Many
laymen
go to them, and these evil men preach the Dharma to those
laymen.
Because of fame
and profit,
they
praise the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. They only seek a living, being slaves
to wealth and
property, greedy for clothing and food, and praising what they themselves delight in, saying:
If one practices giving, one is reborn in heaven.
In the Dharma of the Buddha, giving is an inferior dharma, yet they praise it as the most supreme and say:
The conditions of great giving lead to rebirth in heaven.
They do not understand the Buddha's words and do not comprehend the meaning; they know only the shallow and near inferior dharma of the first stage, cling to self and person, and for-
-sake
the ultimate meaning.

[Caṇḍāla (zhān tuó luó)] A term translated as a savage and evil person, one outside the four castes who makes his living by slaughtering. [Four castes] The four social classes of ancient India: Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra.

Śāriputra, when the Dharma is preached like this, there are sometimes people who give rise to faith and leave home, uniting with those evil people, unable to diligently seek the profound ultimate meaning. Those who have any attainment speak of a self, a person, a life, and a soul, and by thought and discrimination fabricate dharmas that have no reality. In the Abhidharma and the sūtras they set up their own arguments, sometimes speaking of annihilation or permanence, sometimes of a doer, sometimes of no doer.
Śāriputra, when they preach the Dharma like this, sometimes
laymen
give rise to
faith
and

leave home, uniting with those evil people, unable to diligently seek the profound ultimate meaning. They are those who have attainment, speaking of a self, a person, a life, and a soul, and by thought and discrimination fabricate dharmas that have no reality.
Among the scriptures they
do not rely on the Buddha's words but make up their own set, sometimes speaking of annihilation or permanence, sometimes of a doer, sometimes of no doer.
[Abhidharma] The treatises
. [Sūtra (xiū dù lù)] This refers to the sūtras, meaning the scriptures.

Śāriputra, at that time my Dharma was filled with many non-Buddhist dharmas, causing the right-view mind of sentient beings to be destroyed. Thus, Śāriputra, because of these conditions my pure Dharma gradually perishes. Śāriputra, the bodhi that I have long cultivated, undergoing many sufferings amid birth and death, was at that time destroyed by those evil people.

Śāriputra, at that time the Buddha-Dharma was filled with non-Buddhist dharmas, causing the right-view mind of sentient beings to be led astray and fall into wrong views. Thus, Śāriputra, because of these conditions my pure Dharma gradually perishes. Śāriputra, the bodhi path that I have long cultivated amid the endless round of birth and death, undergoing many sufferings, was at that time destroyed by those evil people.

Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu cannot forsake such views of attainment, the view of self, and the view of person, does not understand what the Tathāgata taught adaptively, and yet declares that there is definitively a self and a person, then I do not allow such a person to accept even a single cup of water. Or perhaps when such a person hears the Dharma of emptiness, his faith becomes pure and he is not frightened or doubtful, and then he should turn and guide the multitude into the meaning of reality; he should leave home and receive the full precepts.

Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu cannot forsake such views of attainment, the view of self, and the view of person; does not understand that what the Tathāgata taught adaptively; and yet declares that there is definitively a self and a person, then I do not allow such a person to accept the offering of even a single cup of water.
But if such a person sometimes
hears the Dharma of emptiness, his faith becomes pure and he is not frightened or doubtful,
then he should
guide the multitude into the meaning of reality,
that person
should leave home and receive the full precepts.
[Full precepts (jù zú jiè)] The complete and perfect precepts, such as the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu and the three hundred and forty-eight precepts of a bhikṣuṇī

Why is that? Śāriputra, if a person does not forsake such views, he is called a non-Buddhist. Śāriputra, by worldly conditions I provisionally speak of a self, not as the ultimate meaning. If someone says
I too by worldly conditions speak of a self
If this person can comprehend the dharma of no-birth, no-extinction, and no-marks, and it does not contradict what I have said, he is my disciple.

Why is that? Śāriputra, if a person does not forsake such views of attainment, the view of self, and the view of person, he is called a non-Buddhist. Śāriputra, by worldly conditions I provisionally speak of a self, not
as
the ultimate meaning. If someone says:
I too by worldly conditions speak of a self
If this person can comprehend the dharma of no-
birth,
no-
extinction,
and no-marks, and it does not contradict what I have said, he is my disciple.
Śāriputra, if someone says:

Why does the Tathāgata, following worldly conditions, speak of a self when there is no self? The Tathāgata should not make untrue statements for the sake of the world. Moreover, many scriptures speak of a self; what the Buddha said should not be false.

Śāriputra, one should answer such a person: The Buddha says that all dharmas are empty, without a lord and without a nature; they are but illusions, not the ultimate meaning. The Tathāgata does not, by reason of the ultimate meaning, speak of a self or a person.
Śāriputra, if someone says
“Why does the Tathāgata, following
worldly
conditions,
speak of a self and a person when there is no self? The Tathāgata should not, for the sake of the
world,
make untrue statements. Moreover, many scriptures speak of a self and a person; what the Buddha said should not be false.
Śāriputra, one should answer such a person:
The Buddha says
all dharmas are empty, without a lord and without a nature
, this is the true meaning;
the many scriptures speak of a self
—this is the Buddha, by worldly conditions, provisionally speaking of a self and a person. This is not the ultimate meaning but
the
conventional truth. The Tathāgata does not, by reason of the ultimate
meaning,
speak of a self or a person.

[Two truths] The conventional truth and the true truth. The conventional truth, also called the worldly truth or the conventional truth of the world, is the mundane phenomena seen by ordinary people; the true truth, also called the truth of the ultimate meaning, or the supreme truth, is the real principle seen by noble wisdom, that is, the inwardly realized, speech-transcending dharma-nature.

The words of the noble ones have no attachment, and there is no one of no wisdom who is equal to the Buddha, nor any who surpasses him. Śāriputra, the Tathāgata's wisdom is inconceivable; with this wisdom he knows the minds of sentient beings. How could there be anyone equal to the Buddha? The Buddha is a great dragon,
king of the great Dharma, and one should not object that the Buddha speaks of a self. All the world always contends with me, but I never contend with the world.
The words of the noble ones have no attachment; there is no one without wisdom who could be
equal
to the Buddha, nor anyone who
surpasses
him. Śāriputra, the Tathāgata's wisdom is inconceivable; with
this
wisdom he knows the minds of sentient beings. How could there be anyone
equal
to the Buddha? The Buddha is a great dragon,
king of the great Dharma. One should not
challenge
the Buddha's speaking of a self and a person. All the world always
contends
with
me
but I never contend with the world (because the Buddha, knowing reality, sees that all dharmas are without grasping and without abandoning, without contention and without dispute)
[Níng dāng (宁当)] Does it really mean
[Zhēng (诤)]
To dispute.
Śāriputra, those who speak of a self
are greatly to be pitied. In this there is neither a dharma nor a self; there are many sentient beings who do not understand what the Tathāgata taught adaptively, oppose the Dharma treasure

and fall into many evil destinies. Śāriputra, I know wrong views but am not of wrong views; one who can know wrong views is thereby right view. Śāriputra, wrong views never change into right views, and a view does not know a view.
Śāriputra, those who speak of a self
are greatly to be pitied. In this
ultimate meaning
there is neither a dharma nor a self. There are many sentient beings who do not understand that when the Tathāgata says
there are dharmas and a self
that is
adaptive teaching,
and so
oppose the Dharma treasure
falling into many evil
paths
. Śāriputra, I know wrong views but am not of wrong views; one who can know wrong views is thereby right view. Śāriputra, wrong views never
turn
into right views, and one who holds wrong views cannot
himself
know that they are wrong views.
Śāriputra, the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas is hard to believe in all the world
Among all the gods and the whole world I am the most trustworthy, not untrustworthy.
Śāriputra, the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas is hard
to be-
lieved
Among all the gods
and
the whole world, I am the most trustworthy, not untrustworthy.

Śāriputra, the Dharma I teach is for reaching the other shore, yet in it there is no one who reaches the other shore; the Dharma I teach is for exhausting all formations, yet in it there is no one who exhausts the formations; the Dharma I teach is for the sake of stilling, yet in it there is no one who is stilled; the Dharma I teach is for the sake of extinction, yet in it there is no one who is extinguished; the Dharma I teach is for the sake of liberation, yet in it there is no one who is liberated; the Dharma I teach is for the sake of all wisdoms, yet in it there is no one who has all wisdoms; the Dharma I teach is for the sake of purifying defilement, yet in it there is no one who purifies defilement.
Śāriputra, the Dharma I teach is for reaching
nirvāṇa
, the other shore; in this
ultimate meaning
there is also no one who reaches
nirvāṇa
, the other shore. The Dharma I teach is for
exhausting
all formations; in this
ultimate meaning
there is also no one who
exhausts
the formations. The Dharma I teach is for the sake of stilling
—the
reason being that in this
ultimate meaning
there is also no one who is stilled. The Dharma I teach is for the sake of extinction
—the
reason being that in this
ultimate meaning
there is also no one who is extinguished. The Dharma I teach is for the sake of liberation
—the
reason being that in this
ultimate meaning
there is also no one who is liberated. The Dharma I teach is for the sake of all wisdoms
—the
reason being that in this
ultimate meaning
there is also no one who has all wisdoms. The Dharma I teach is for the sake of purifying
and re-
-moving
defilement
—the
reason being that in this
ultimate meaning
there is also no one who purifies and re-
-moves
defilement.
[Extinction (miè dù)] This is nirvāṇa. To extin-
-guish
is to exhaust the three delusions of views and thoughts, dust-like defilements, and ignorance
to cross over
is to pass beyond the two kinds of birth-and-death, the fragmented and the transformational. [All wisdoms (zhū zhì)]
the various
wisdoms that deeply understand the nature of things

Śāriputra, the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for the gods, yet there are no gods; he preaches the Dharma for people, yet there are no people; he preaches the Dharma for sentient beings, yet there are no sentient beings. Śāriputra, the Tathāgata speaks of clarity and liberation, yet in this there is no clarity and no liberation. I speak of Buddha-recitation, yet the Buddha cannot be thought of; I speak of the practice of emptiness, yet emptiness cannot be practiced, nor can it be thought of. Śāriputra, this is called the passages of scripture taught by the Tathāgata, and in them there is no speaker. Evil people seize these passages and preach them to others, and also take me as their teacher, without the virtues of the Tathāgata's noble assembly, yet counting themselves among the Saṅgha.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for the
assembly of
gods, yet there are no
gods;
he preaches the Dharma for the
assembly of
people, yet there are no
people;
he preaches the Dharma for sentient beings, yet there are no sentient beings. Śāriputra, the Tathāgata speaks of clarity and liberation, and in this
ultimate meaning
there
is also
no clarity
and
no liberation. I speak of Buddha-recitation, yet the Buddha cannot be thought of; I speak of the practice of emptiness, yet emptiness cannot be practiced, nor can it be thought of. Śāriputra,
these are

the passages of scripture taught by the Tathāgata, and in them there is no speaker. Evil people seize these passages and preach them to others, taking me as their teacher, but they do not have the virtues of the Tathāgata's noble assembly, yet count themselves
as
members of the Saṅgha.
[Clarity (míng)] Another name for wisdom.

Śāriputra, just as a troop of monkeys does not resemble the Trāyastriṃśa gods, so those many evil people do not resemble my noble assembly. Śāriputra, those evil people call themselves śramaṇas merely by voice and speech, just like the foolish man who saw a troop of monkeys and took them for the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Śāriputra,
just as

a troop of monkeys does not resemble the Trāyastriṃśa gods, so those many evil people do not resemble my noble assembly. Śāriputra, those evil people, merely by voice and speech, say they are śramaṇas, just like the foolish man who saw a troop of monkeys and said these were the Trāyastriṃśa gods.

Śāriputra, among them there are monks who delight in questioning and disputation. If they meet a good teacher who teaches them that name-and-form is stilled, that the path of words is cut off, that there is no arising and no loss, and that they penetrate the signless, and if upon hearing such Dharma of no-birth, no-extinction, and no-signs they are not frightened or awed, then one should know that this person has already made offerings to countless Buddhas, can know my Dharma, and may be called the noble assembly.
Śāriputra, among them there are monks who delight in
questioning and disputation
, and who meet
a good

teacher who teaches them that name-and-form is stilled, that the path of words is cut off, that there is no arising and no loss, and that they penetrate the signless. If upon hearing such Dharma of no-birth, no-extinction, and no-signs
they
are not frightened or awed, then one should know that this person has already made offerings to countless Buddhas, can know my Dharma, and may be called the noble assembly.
[Name-and-form] The general name for the five aggregates. Of the five aggregates,
the
four aggregates of feeling, conception, formations, and consciousness constitute name, and the aggregate of form constitutes form.
In this chapter the World-Honored One reveals what impure Dharma-preaching is, and how fearsome impure Dharma-preaching is.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: In the past, Kashyapa Buddha
(the same as the character 'beforehand')
made a prediction about me, saying: Because Śākyamuni Buddha will receive many offerings, the Dharma will soon perish. Śāriputra, my Dharma will indeed, because of many offerings, soon perish later.

The Buddha said to Śāriputra: In the past, when Kashyapa Buddha made a prediction about me, he said: Because Śākyamuni Buddha will receive many offerings, the Dharma will soon perish. Śāriputra, my Dharma will indeed, because of many offerings, soon perish later.

[Kashyapa Buddha] The Buddha immediately preceding Śākyamuni Buddha, one of the Seven Buddhas. [Seven Buddhas] In the great eon (the eon of the wise) in which we now live, seven Buddhas have appeared: Vipāśyin Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, Viśvabhū Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kashyapa Buddha, and Śākyamuni Buddha.

Śāriputra, just as a poor man who obtains a great treasure feels great joy in his heart, so, Śāriputra, in a future age there will be many bhikṣus who draw near to laymen, receive their offerings, gradually become intimate with them and act as their servants, and their hearts rejoice and delight, just like the poor man who obtains a great treasure. Such foolish people prize worldly profit and joy, becoming servants of worldly pleasures. If they see a bhikṣu receiving many offerings, they think he has attained arhatship; if they see one with few acquaintances, they call him an evil person. Such bhikṣus, for the sake of profit and support, forsake the supreme Buddha-path and, following what is pleasing, accomplish that matter.

Śāriputra, just as a poor man who obtains a great treasure feels great joy in his heart, so, Śāriputra, in a future age there will be many bhikṣus who draw near to laymen (white-robed householders), receive their offerings, gradually become intimate with them and act as their servants (to please them), and their hearts rejoice in these offerings and delight, just like the poor man who obtains a great treasure. Such foolish people willingly become servants for the sake of worldly fame, profit, and worldly pleasures. If people see a bhikṣu receiving many offerings, they think he has already attained arhatship; but if they see a bhikṣu who receives few offerings, they call him an evil person. These bhikṣus who are greedy for worldly profit and pleasure, for the sake of receiving many offerings, forsake the supreme Buddha-path and preach the scriptures according to the preferences of the laymen.
[And act as their servants] By the monastic rule, a bhikṣu must not serve a layman; he should convert through the Dharma and live purely by himself.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata now speaks such scriptures for those foolish people. Why? Because a precept-breaking bhikṣu, upon hearing this scripture

will give rise to repentance and should return to keeping the precepts, not becoming a great thief who receives the offerings of others. Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu hears this scripture and his mind is not pure, not rejoicing, not delighting, then he is called a corrupt and evil bhikṣu. Why? Śāriputra, a bhikṣu of pure precepts delights in every Dharma, whether it speaks of giving, of keeping precepts, of patience, of diligence, of meditation, of wisdom, or of such fearful scriptures
his mind rejoices in all of them.

Śāriputra, the Tathāgata now speaks this scripture (the Buddha-treasure scripture) for those foolish people. Why? Because a precept-breaking bhikṣu, upon hearing this scripture, gives rise to repentance, returns to keeping the precepts, and does not become a great thief receiving their offerings. Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu hears this scripture and his mind is not pure, not rejoicing, not delighting, then he is called a corrupt and evil bhikṣu. Why? Śāriputra, a bhikṣu of pure precepts delights in every Dharma of this scripture (because he deeply understands the World-Honored One's compassionate intent to save them, feels the Buddha's compassion, and feels the Buddha's great kindness), whether it speaks of giving, of keeping precepts, of patience, of diligence, of meditation, of wisdom, or of such fearful scriptures that make corrupt and evil bhikṣus afraid — in all of them his mind greatly rejoices.

Śāriputra, there are three kinds of people who, upon hearing this scripture, are troubled and distressed. Which three? First, the precept-breaking bhikṣu; second, the person of overweening pride; third, the one who preaches impurely. Moreover, there are three more kinds of people who, upon hearing such a scripture, are troubled and distressed. Which three? First, the view of a person; second, the view of a life; third, the view of a self.

Śāriputra, there are three kinds of people who, upon hearing this scripture (the Buddha-treasure scripture), are troubled and distressed. Which three kinds of people? First, the precept-breaking bhikṣu; second, the person of overweening pride; third, the one who preaches impurely. And there are three more kinds of people who, upon hearing such a scripture, are troubled and distressed. Which three? First, those who hold the view of a person; second, those who hold the view of a life; third, those who hold the view of a self.
